content.title: About
content.content: Cooked carrots are the root vegetable that has been boiled or steamed until tender. Most nutrients are retained during cooking, while the natural sugars become sweeter and the texture softens. Cooked carrots are common in soups, stews, salads, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Carrots have been cultivated for over 5,000 years, originating in Central Asia.
The orange variety was developed in the Netherlands in the 17th century through selective breeding.
Raw carrots can be purple, yellow, red, or white; orange became dominant due to its high beta‑carotene content.
Cooking makes beta‑carotene more bioavailable for conversion to vitamin A.
Carrots are used in traditional medicine to support vision and immune health.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene converts to vitamin A, essential for eye health, skin, and immune function.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Fiber and potassium help regulate blood pressure and cholesterol levels.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Carotenoids and vitamin C protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Both soluble and insoluble fiber promote healthy gut motility.

items.title: May reduce chronic disease risk
items.content: Regular carrot consumption is linked to lower risk of certain cancers and type 2 diabetes.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience an allergic reaction to carrots.

items.title: Excess vitamin A
items.content: Very large intakes of carrots can lead to hypervitaminosis A, causing a yellowish skin tone.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: People with sensitive stomachs may experience gas when eating large amounts of cooked carrots.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked carrots can be served as a side, added to salads, purees, soups, and stews. They are also used in baking (e.g., carrot cake) and in juices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked carrots in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3–5 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags to retain flavor and nutrients.

content.title: About
content.content: Raw fig is a sweet, juicy fruit of the fig tree (Ficus carica) native to the Mediterranean, parts of Asia, and the United States. The fruit has a soft flesh covered by a thin edible skin and contains tiny edible seeds. Figs are eaten fresh and also used in desserts, salads, and preserves.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fig belongs to the mulberry family and is one of the oldest cultivated fruits, grown for over 5,000 years.
The edible fruit develops from an inverted flower inside a structure called a syconium, not from external blossoms.
There are more than 200 fig varieties, differing in flesh color, flavor, and size.
In ancient Egypt, Greece, and Rome, figs were called the “fruit of the gods.”
Fig seeds are rich in fiber and healthy fats.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Figs provide both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and blood sugar regulation.

items.title: Source of vitamin K
items.content: Raw figs contain vitamin K, which is important for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and polyphenols in figs help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Potassium and magnesium in figs contribute to normal blood pressure and heart function.

items.title: Provides essential minerals
items.content: Figs are a good source of calcium, iron, and magnesium, needed for bones and blood formation.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to figs, especially if they are allergic to other mulberry family plants.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Fresh figs contain a notable amount of natural sugars, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: Large amounts of figs can cause gas and discomfort due to their high fiber content.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw figs can be eaten as a snack, added to salads, yogurts, oatmeal, and used in baking, jams, and sauces. Before eating, rinse the fruit and optionally peel the skin.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store figs in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 5–7 days. For longer storage, freeze the fruit after removing the skin.

content.title: About
content.content: Cooked green pepper is the mature fruit of the sweet pepper plant (Capsicum annuum) that, after heat treatment, retains a bright color, tender texture, and a mildly sweet flavor. It is commonly used as an ingredient in soups, stews, salads, and side dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green peppers are harvested before full ripening, making them less sweet than red or yellow peppers.
Cooking increases the bioavailability of certain antioxidants such as vitamin C and carotenoids.
In cuisine, cooked green pepper is often used for stuffed peppers and sauces.
Different regions have their own names: in the US it’s called "green bell pepper", in Spain "pimiento verde".

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Cooked green pepper retains a high amount of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Carotenoids and flavonoids help combat free radicals, reducing the risk of chronic diseases.

items.title: Low‑calorie source of fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety while the pepper remains low in calories.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B6 and folate are involved in protein metabolism and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure, contributing to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pepper, manifested as skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Food interactions
items.content: Large amounts of pepper may affect the action of certain medications, such as anticoagulants, due to its vitamin K content.

items.title: Sodium excess
items.content: If the pepper is prepared with added salt, total sodium intake should be monitored.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked green pepper can be added to soups, stews, pasta, salads, used as a filling for stuffed vegetables, or served as a side dish. It is convenient to dice or slice it.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked green pepper in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags.

content.title: About
content.content: Kefir is a tangy, slightly fizzy fermented milk drink made by adding kefir grains, which are small colonies of bacteria and yeasts, to milk. It originated in the North Caucasus and is popular in Eastern Europe, Central Asia, and increasingly around the world. Kefir has a thin, drinkable texture and is consumed on its own, in smoothies, and in cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Kefir originated in the North Caucasus region and has been made for centuries.
Kefir grains look like small clumps of cauliflower and are used again and again to make new batches.
Kefir contains a wider variety of microorganisms than most yogurts, including both bacteria and yeasts.
Fermentation lowers the lactose content compared with milk.
Kefir can also be made with plant-based drinks, and water kefir is a separate, non-dairy fermented drink.

items.title: Contains live cultures
items.content: Kefir provides live bacteria and yeasts that may support digestive health.

items.title: Provides protein and calcium
items.content: Kefir provides protein and calcium, which support muscles, bones, and teeth.

items.title: Provides B vitamins
items.content: Kefir contains vitamin B12 and riboflavin (B2).

items.title: May be easier to digest than milk
items.content: Microbes in kefir break down some lactose, so many people with mild lactose intolerance tolerate it better.

items.title: Versatile
items.content: Kefir can replace buttermilk or yogurt in many recipes and drinks.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Dairy kefir contains milk protein and should be avoided by people allergic to milk.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Kefir still contains some lactose and may cause discomfort in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Digestive adjustment
items.content: Kefir may cause gas or bloating when you first start drinking it, so introduce it gradually.

items.title: Weakened immunity, sugar, and medications
items.content: People with weakened immunity should ask a healthcare professional about live-culture products. Flavored kefir can contain added sugar, and calcium in dairy can reduce the absorption of some medications.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Kefir can be drunk on its own, blended into smoothies, poured over cereal, or used in pancakes, baking, salad dressings, and cold soups. Plain kefir can be flavored with fruit or honey. It can replace buttermilk in many recipes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep kefir refrigerated and use it by the date on the package. After opening, close the container tightly and use it within about a week. It continues to ferment and become more sour over time. Discard kefir that smells bad or has mold.

content.title: About
content.content: Peanut sauce is a thick sauce made from ground peanuts, often combined with soy sauce, vinegar, sugar, garlic and spices. It is a staple in Asian cuisines, especially Thai, Indonesian and Vietnamese, where it is used as a dip, salad dressing, meat marinate and noodle topping.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: In Thailand the sauce is called “satay” and in Indonesia “sambal” when mixed with peanuts.
Traditional recipes toast the peanuts first, giving the sauce a deep nutty aroma and creamy texture.
Vegans and vegetarians often rely on it for plant‑based protein and healthy fats.
There are many variations: sweet‑spicy, coconut‑milk based, lime‑infused, or ginger‑spiked.
Peanut sauce can be bought ready‑made or prepared at home in just a few minutes.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Peanuts provide about 25 % protein, making the sauce a good protein source for plant‑based diets.

items.title: Contains mono‑ and polyunsaturated fats
items.content: These fats support heart health and can help lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The sauce supplies niacin, thiamine and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Peanuts are a source of magnesium, phosphorus and potassium, which aid nerve and muscle function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Resveratrol and vitamin E in peanuts help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanuts are a strong allergen; reactions can be severe and require medical attention.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Because of its fat content, the sauce is calorie‑rich; portion control is advisable.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Store‑bought versions often contain a lot of salt; low‑sodium options are better for people with hypertension.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Some recipes add considerable sugar, which can affect blood glucose levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use peanut sauce as a dip for vegetables, spring rolls and shrimp, as a salad dressing, as a marinate for chicken, beef or tofu, or stir it into soups and noodle dishes. It can be served warm or cold.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the sauce in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks. For longer storage, freeze in small portions; thaw and stir well before use. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or mold.

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of lean pork, boiled or roasted potatoes, and a mix of vegetables – carrots, broccoli and dark‑green leafy greens (spinach, kale, etc.). It is prepared without sauces, preserving the natural flavors of the ingredients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pork is a good source of high‑quality protein and vitamin B12.
Potatoes are one of the world’s most consumed root vegetables; they are rich in potassium and vitamin C.
Broccoli contains sulforaphane, a compound with antioxidant properties.
Carrots are high in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Dark‑green leafy vegetables such as spinach and kale provide large amounts of vitamins K, A and folate.

items.title: Supports muscle mass
items.content: Protein from pork helps build and repair muscle tissue.

items.title: Helps lower blood pressure
items.content: Potassium in potatoes and vegetables aids in maintaining fluid‑electrolyte balance.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Broccoli, carrots and leafy greens are rich in antioxidants that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Promotes eye health
items.content: Beta‑carotene from carrots and vitamin A support healthy vision.

items.title: Strengthens bones
items.content: Vitamin K from leafy greens and calcium from small amounts in pork contribute to bone mineralization.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Some cuts of pork can be high in saturated fat; choose lean cuts whenever possible.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Adding salt or using pre‑made seasonings can increase sodium intake.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals may have an allergic reaction to pork.

items.title: Potential pathogens
items.content: Pork must be cooked thoroughly to eliminate risks of salmonella and trichinella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, cutting pork into bite‑size pieces, potatoes into cubes or wedges, and lightly sautéing or steaming the vegetables. Fresh herbs such as parsley or dill can be added for extra aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Freeze for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Flour taco shells are thin, crispy shells made from enriched wheat flour, water, salt, and vegetable oil. They are designed for quick preparation of tacos, burritos, and other Mexican dishes. The shell has a mild, neutral flavor that highlights the fillings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Flour tortillas became popular in the United States in the early 20th century as a cheaper alternative to corn shells.
Traditionally they are formed as 10‑12 cm diameter circles and fried until golden.
Flour shells soften faster in the microwave than corn shells, making them easier to use.
They are often called “flour taco shell” to distinguish them from “corn taco shell.”
Whole‑grain versions add a nuttier taste and extra fiber.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Provides a quick source of energy thanks to easily digestible carbs.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Enriched flour supplies iron, important for blood formation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Includes thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with corn shells, flour shells usually contain less fat when no extra oil is added.

items.title: Versatile flavor
items.content: Neutral taste makes it suitable for a wide range of diets, including vegetarian and gluten‑free (when made with gluten‑free flour).

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: Contains gluten, so it is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Rapid carbohydrate absorption can raise blood sugar, which is important for diabetics.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some brands add salt; choose low‑sodium versions if you monitor sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Warm the shell briefly in the oven, microwave, or skillet, then fill with meat, fish, beans, vegetables, cheese, and sauces. It also works well for casseroles, chips, and mini‑pizzas.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a sealed package. After opening, use within 1‑2 weeks. For longer storage keep in the refrigerator, but keep moisture out to prevent softening.
